title: Replacement Through Knowledge Acquisition
gist: Frontier AI labs that supply inference to enterprises can extract information from customer prompts, files, outputs and behavior and use it to build capabilities and vertically enter their customers' own markets—a dynamic the authors call 'replacement through knowledge acquisition' (RKA). They argue existing legal tools (contracts, trade secrets, antitrust) are all inadequate to prevent it, and that enterprises and regulators should prepare optionality now.

insights.claim: A small number of frontier AI labs supplying inference to millions of enterprises can extract information from customer AI usage and leverage it to compete directly in those customers' own markets—a threat the authors label 'replacement through knowledge acquisition' (RKA).
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Enterprises that embed a single vendor's models into core workflows are handing that vendor the raw material to eventually replace them; treat AI vendor lock-in as a competitive, not just operational, risk.
insights.quote: Enterprises must protect themselves from “replacement through knowledge acquisition” (RKA)—from being consumed, digested, and replaced by frontier AI labs.
insights.locator: RKA Is a Threat to Enterprises

insights.claim: AI labs currently claim not to train on enterprise inputs, but as their market power grows they have strong incentives to alter or circumvent that commitment to widen the capability gap over open-weight alternatives and deepen customer dependency.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Vendor no-train promises are contingent on market structure, not permanent guarantees—discount them as the labs gain pricing and dependency leverage.
insights.quote: These labs currently claim not to train their models on inputs from enterprise customers, yet they have strong incentives to alter or circumvent that commitment as their market power grows.

insights.claim: The industries most exposed to RKA are those where information shared with AI providers directly implicates their own products—software, legal, and financial services—because usage data there can most plausibly be turned into competing products.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Software, law, and finance firms feeding proprietary code, legal strategy, or investment strategy into shared frontier models are the first-order RKA targets to watch.
insights.quote: The industries most vulnerable to RKA are those in which information shared with AI providers directly implicates the industries’ products or services—for instance, software or legal.
insights.locator: RKA Is a Threat to Enterprises

insights.claim: Aggregating the AI usage of many employees within one enterprise can reveal far more about that firm than any single employee can access, because linked and synthesized inputs expose the organization as a whole.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The aggregation risk means even benign individual prompts collectively leak strategic information—governance of company-wide AI use, not just sensitive queries, is the exposure surface.
insights.quote: if many employees within the same enterprise are using the same AI models simultaneously, the available information, once linked and synthesized, could reveal much more about the enterprise than any single employee has access to.
insights.locator: RKA Is a Threat to Enterprises

insights.claim: As AI moves beyond text interfaces into ambient note-takers, embedded agents, augmented reality, and deployed industrial robots, the surface for data extraction expands to eventually threaten even manufacturing incumbents.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: RKA is not confined to knowledge work—firms licensing embedded AI hardware (robots, AR, wearables) should assume the device is also a data-collection channel.
insights.quote: deployed industrial robots can be used as data collection devices, extending the threat of RKA to industries like manufacturing, where incumbents may license robots only to have their industrial information appropriated by them.
insights.locator: RKA Is a Threat to Enterprises

insights.claim: High AI-lab valuations can only be sustained by high growth and eventually high profits, creating structural pressure to find new data, better models, and new markets—which points labs toward owning downstream uses rather than merely servicing them.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The same valuation math that supports the AI trade is what pushes labs to encroach on their customers—growth expectations make vertical expansion nearly inevitable.
insights.quote: High valuations can be sustained only with high growth and eventually high profits.
insights.locator: RKA Is a Threat to Enterprises

insights.claim: As OpenAI adds features to flagship products like ChatGPT, standalone startups are already being replaced by the AI labs themselves, and enterprise CEOs including Microsoft's Satya Nadella and Palantir's Alex Karp are publicly warning of power concentrating in a few labs.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The replacement dynamic is already visible in the startup layer and named by major-cap CEOs—a signal that AI-application companies face platform-risk repricing.
insights.quote: the CEOs of larger enterprises—such as Microsoft’s Satya Nadella and Palantir’s Alex Karp—are waking up to the peril, warning companies of a growing concentration of power in a small number of AI labs.

insights.claim: Enterprises face a Scylla-or-Charybdis choice: adopt frontier models and risk RKA, or forgo the frontier and risk being outcompeted by better-equipped rivals.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: There is no clean opt-out—both adopting and abstaining carry competitive cost, which is why the authors push toward legal and architectural defenses instead.
insights.quote: Embrace frontier models and risk RKA, or forgo the frontier and risk being outmatched by better-equipped competitors.

insights.claim: The unit economics of AI—high up-front costs, low marginal deployment costs—plus technological flywheels like recursive self-improvement make a future of individual labs holding vast market power a scenario to take seriously.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: If flywheels concentrate power, open-weight and in-house models may cease to be viable competitive substitutes—raising the odds of coercive data terms.

insights.claim: RKA can occur along two axes—overt vs. covert acquisition, and isolated training runs (which require long-term data retention) vs. continual learning (which updates models from transient interactions without retention)—yielding four distinct modes.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A four-quadrant map for auditing vendor risk: the hardest to detect is covert extraction via continual learning, which leaves no retained dataset to inspect.

insights.claim: Continual-learning methods that update models directly from transient customer interactions would blur the line between product use and model development, making it easier for labs to leverage customer information without detection.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Data-retention audits lose their teeth if training no longer requires retention—detection frameworks must evolve with the training paradigm.
insights.quote: as training methods evolve, the line between product use and model development will be blurred, and it will become easier for labs to leverage customer information without detection.

insights.claim: Structural limits may blunt RKA: the knowledge needed to compete in a new market may be tacit and impossible to reconstruct from inputs, and customers can adopt private clouds, open-weight models, or unlinkable inference to raise the difficulty.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Architecture choices—private cloud, open weights, unlinkable inference—are a concrete defensive lever enterprises can pull now, before legal remedies mature.

insights.claim: Anthropic's leading frontier model Fable 5 is already unavailable to organizations with zero data retention (ZDR) enabled, showing that a peerless model can be used to change information-retention policies even when the lab claims retention is only for safety.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete precedent that model superiority is already being used to condition data terms—exactly the coercion mechanism the RKA thesis predicts.
insights.quote: the current leading frontier model from Anthropic, Fable 5, is already not available to organizations with zero data retention (ZDR) enabled.

insights.claim: Existing AI no-train promises are vague and insufficient: OpenAI's enterprise agreement says it 'will not use Customer Content to develop or improve the Services' and Anthropic's says it 'may not train models on Customer Content,' but both leave 'Customer Content,' 'develop or improve,' and 'train' undefined.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The contractual carve-outs are wide enough to permit derivative, deidentified, or non-'response' data uses—enterprises relying on standard AI terms have weaker protection than they assume.
insights.quote: OpenAI will not use Customer Content to develop or improve the Services, unless Customer explicitly agrees to such use.

insights.claim: Because only labs know what data they use for training, enterprise customers cannot reliably detect a data breach absent whistleblowing or transparency requirements.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The detection asymmetry is the crux: without mandated transparency, contractual protections are effectively unenforceable because breaches are invisible.
insights.quote: data breaches by AI providers are nearly impossible for enterprise customers to reliably identify because only the AI labs themselves know exactly what data is used for model training.

insights.claim: Anthropic has published methods for 'conversation distillation'—turning deidentified customer inputs into categorized usage clusters—illustrating how derivative data not shown to the user as a 'response' could fall outside contractual output definitions.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Shows a live technique that plausibly sits in the contractual gray zone—enterprises should push to define 'customer content' to cover inferred and synthesized data, not just inputs and outputs.
insights.quote: Anthropic has even published methods for conversation distillation—that is, taking deidentified customer inputs and distilling them into categorized usage clusters.

insights.claim: The authors argue AI contracts should flip from enumerating prohibited uses to enumerating permitted uses—disallowing any non-listed activity—and broaden 'customer content' to cover all inputted, inferred, imputed, or synthesized information.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete negotiating playbook for enterprise counsel: permitted-use whitelists plus broad content definitions close the gray areas that prohibited-use lists leave open.
insights.quote: rather than enumerating prohibited uses (for example, “Anthropic does not train models”), agreements should enumerate permitted uses (for instance, “Anthropic can monitor the number of tokens generated by models”), disallowing any non-enumerated activity.

insights.claim: Trade secret law poorly fits RKA because the value of enterprise AI data is usually gestalt—an aggregated set of non-secret knowledge valuable in context—rather than specific, particularized secrets that trade secret doctrine requires.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Firms should not assume trade secret litigation will recover value lost to RKA; the diffuse nature of prompt/behavior data falls between doctrinal cracks.
insights.quote: it is more likely that the true value of enterprise information is gestalt—an aggregated set of non-secret, generalized knowledge that is economically valuable not due to its secret status, but rather due to its specific application in context.

insights.claim: If a misappropriated secret is encoded directly into model weights, remedy is hard because 'machine unlearning' remains far more difficult than deleting data from a database, making full model deletion a disproportionate and unlikely remedy.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Even a winning trade-secret plaintiff may get only forced royalties, not disgorgement—weak deterrence against baking data into weights.
insights.quote: deleting information from a model is still far harder to do than deleting information from a database.

insights.claim: U.S. antitrust cannot reach RKA: the Sherman Act polices exclusion of rivals, not exploitation of customers, so conditioning model access on permissive data sharing is treated as a lab's private right, and vertical entry into a customer's market reads as pro-competitive.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Antitrust offers a catch-22 with no ex ante or ex post remedy—don't expect U.S. competition enforcement to protect AI application incumbents.
insights.quote: the Sherman Act polices only exclusion of rivals, not exploitation of customers, and thus contains no protections against RKA as a form of exploitative abuse.

insights.claim: In the EU, exploitation itself is a cognizable offense—as in the Amazon Marketplace case where Amazon allegedly used nonpublic seller data to compete, later codified into the Digital Markets Act—but the DMA left AI services off its regulated list, so EU law will do little against RKA.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The Amazon case is 'RKA in miniature' but the DMA's AI carve-out plus slow, weakly enforced remedies mean EU regulation is not a near-term backstop either.
insights.quote: Amazon was accused of using nonpublic business data from sellers to calibrate its own retail decisions and compete directly with the sellers—RKA in miniature.

insights.claim: Because model providers know which customers negotiated strong data protections while those customers don't, a safe harbor letting companies share negotiated data-protection terms—modeled on the 1984 National Cooperative Research Act—could offset the labs' informational advantage.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A low-cost policy lever: collective term-sharing raises the floor on enterprise protections without heavy-handed AI regulation.
insights.quote: Model providers know which companies have negotiated strong contractual protections, but the companies that lack such protections don’t.

insights.claim: Training-data transparency and third-party auditing—already foreshadowed by the EU AI Act's technical-documentation requirements—would resolve the core RKA problem that only labs know what data trains their models.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Transparency mandates are the single highest-leverage fix because they convert an undetectable breach into an auditable one.
insights.quote: only the labs themselves know exactly what information is being used to train their models.

insights.claim: Regulators could impose a duty on AI providers not to misuse customer data absent consent—mirroring telecom rules that bar carriers from using 'customer proprietary network information' for their own lines of business.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A ready statutory template exists in telecom CPNI rules—codifying private no-train commitments into an enforceable duty.
insights.quote: carriers may not use “customer proprietary network information”—that is, the knowledge they inevitably derive from carrying customers’ traffic—for their own marketing or other lines of business without consent.

insights.claim: California would matter disproportionately to any RKA statutory-damages regime, having already enacted training-data disclosure and limited per-consumer statutory damages.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Watch California as the venue where AI data-use liability first gains teeth—state-level per-violation damages could shift lab incentives before federal action.
insights.quote: California would matter disproportionately in any such effort, and it has already enacted versions of training-data disclosure and limited per-consumer statutory damages.

insights.claim: The authors counsel a wait-and-prepare stance: premature RKA regulation risks stifling innovation ('wasp spray on a honeybee hive') while acting too late risks a large share of the economy falling under a few labs.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The policy recommendation is optionality, not immediate rules—so near-term enterprise defense rests on contracts and architecture, not regulation.
insights.quote: the path now should be forward: warily watching the growing power of AI labs and laying the foundation for legal and regulatory responses to RKA if—or when—the time comes.
